To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the announcement of the FE failure triggered negative stock-price reactions at other insurers, (2) these reactions are stronger for insurers with greater retail business, and (3) the reactions to the FE failure announcement are conditioned on the extent of the firm’s junk-bond holdings.

the stock market reacts negatively to the First Executive Corporation (FE) announcement of an accounting loss on junk bonds, that the reaction is stronger for insurers with larger holdings of junk bonds or more dependence on retail business and that the reaction is weaker for insurers that are more dependent on institutional investors.

the First Executive failure was associated with a decline in the value of life insurers with junk bonds in their portfolios, and that this decline was larger for companies with more retail policyholders.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of a major financial failure on the stock prices of other firms in the same industry.
the impact of a large life insurer's financial crisis on other life insurers.
the effects of the junk bond problems at First Executive on the stock prices of other life insurers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the stock price reactions are not random, but are related to the degree of retail business dependence, the degree of junk bond holdings, and to the degree of media coverage of the FE problems.
the FE failure did not trigger a generalized market reaction.

the FE announcement of a junk-bond charge had a significant negative effect on the stock prices of other life insurers, and that the effect was conditioned on both the degree of junk bonds held by the insurer and the extent of its retail business.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
retail policyholder reactions are not indiscriminate.
the FE failure has had a significant impact on the life insurance industry, but that the effect has not been as severe as many have feared.
the stock market reaction of life insurance companies to the First Executive Corporation crisis is a function of their junk-bond exposure and their dependence on retail customers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the event of an industry-wide failure, realistic, balanced communication about the condition of an insurer targeted toward individual policyholders will be useful in mitigating a surge in policyholder withdrawals.
the effects of financial crises in the insurance industry are not limited to the firms that experience the crisis, and can affect other firms, even in unrelated business lines.
the financial crisis at First Executive Corporation in 1991 was a watershed event for the life insurance industry.
